items.basis: The proposed radiative cooling surface cannot function independently of humidity in the way claimed because radiative cooling requires a clear view to the sky, which is impossible in a vaccine storage vessel that must be enclosed to protect contents from environmental contamination and physical damage.

The solution fails to address the critical boundary condition of water-wick channel clogging with dissolved salts, which would still occur regardless of radiative cooling capability and would eventually compromise both cooling mechanisms.

The candidate's evidence includes a study on chemical storage tanks (doi:10.1016/j.renene.2023.04.141) which is irrelevant to vaccine storage as it deals with evaporative loss control rather than temperature maintenance, and another paper about cooled ceilings and MPCM slurry (doi:10.1109/icise.2010.5689312) which is an active cooling system, not passive.

Incorporating a radiative cooling surface that selectively emits in the 8-13 μm range while reflecting solar radiation would require precise manufacturing and material science capabilities that are incompatible with the low-cost, mass production requirements for last-mile clinic equipment in resource-limited settings.

The testable prediction fails to pin down the critical variable of cooling margin remaining before vaccine spoilage, instead only measuring "cooling duration" which doesn't provide the temporal precision needed to determine when vaccines are at risk of exceeding the 8°C threshold.
